claim: Maternal loss of imprinting (LOI) at the H19/IGF2 locus results in biallelic IGF2 and reduced H19 expression and is associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS).
source: Maternal loss of imprinting (LOI) at the H19/IGF2 locus results in biallelic IGF2 and reduced H19 expression and is associated with Beckwith–-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS).
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that cites established medical knowledge about BWS and references the molecular phenotype.

claim: Neonatal cardiomegaly in LOI mouse models is exclusively dependent on increased Igf2.
source: Here we focus on cardiovascular phenotypes and show that neonatal cardiomegaly is exclusively dependent on increased Igf2.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments described in the manuscript comparing different mouse models.

claim: Circulating IGF2 binds cardiomyocyte receptors to hyperactivate mTOR signaling, resulting in cellular hyperplasia and hypertrophy.
source: Circulating IGF2 binds cardiomyocyte receptors to hyperactivate mTOR signaling, resulting in cellular hyperplasia and hypertrophy.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data showing increased phosphorylated AKT and S6K1 in LOI hearts, and by experiments with IGF2 peptide treatment.

claim: Igf2-dependent cardiac phenotypes are transient and cardiac size returns to normal once Igf2 expression is suppressed postnatally.
source: These Igf2-dependent phenotypes are transient: cardiac size returns to normal once Igf2 expression is suppressed postnatally.
evidence: This is supported by measurements showing that by 2 months of age, heart weight/tibia length ratios were not significantly different between LOI and wild-type mice.

claim: Reduced H19 expression is sufficient to cause progressive heart pathologies including fibrosis and reduced ventricular function.
source: However, reduced H19 expression is sufficient to cause progressive heart pathologies including fibrosis and reduced ventricular function.
evidence: This is supported by data from H19ΔEx1/H19+ mice showing cardiac pathologies despite normal Igf2 expression.

claim: In the heart, H19 expression is primarily in endothelial cells (ECs).
source: In the heart, H19 expression is primarily in endothelial cells (ECs) and regulates EC differentiation both in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data showing H19 expression overlapping with endothelial markers.

claim: H19 regulates EC differentiation both in vivo and in vitro.
source: In the heart, H19 expression is primarily in endothelial cells (ECs) and regulates EC differentiation both in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic analyses of isolated endothelial cells and transfection experiments.

claim: Cardiac phenotypes in LOI mice depend on H19 lncRNA interactions with Mirlet7 microRNAs.
source: Finally, we establish novel mouse models to show that cardiac phenotypes depend on H19 lncRNA interactions with Mirlet7 microRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by data from H19ΔLet7 mice showing cardiac pathologies when Mirlet7 binding sites are deleted.

claim: There are 100-200 imprinted genes in mammals.
source: There are 100–200 imprinted genes in mammals.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about imprinted genes.

claim: Imprinted genes are organized into discrete clusters where monoallelic expression is dependent on a shared regulatory element known as the Imprinting Control Region (ICR).
source: These genes are organized into discrete clusters where monoallelic expression is dependent on a shared regulatory element known as the Imprinting Control Region (ICR) (Barlow and Bartolomei, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Imprinted genes are frequently involved in human disease and developmental disorders.
source: Imprinted genes are frequently involved in human disease and developmental disorders (Eggermann et al., 2015; Feinberg and Tycko, 2004; Horsthemke, 2014; Kalish et al., 2014; Peters, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The H19ICR is located just upstream of the H19 promoter.
source: Imprinting in this >100 kb region is determined by the H19ICR, located just upstream of the H19 promoter (Kaffer et al., 2000; Thorvaldsen et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The H19ICR organizes the locus such that transcription of the IGF2 and H19 genes are restricted to the paternal and maternal chromosomes, respectively.
source: As described in Figure 1A, the H19ICR organizes the locus such that transcription of the IGF2 (Insulin-like Growth Factor 2) and H19 genes are restricted to the paternal and maternal chromosomes, respectively (Ideraabdullah et al., 2008; Murrell, 2011; Yoon et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: IGF2 encodes a peptide hormone that binds to and activates the insulin receptor (InsR) and insulin-like growth factor one receptor (Igf1R) kinases.
source: IGF2 encodes a peptide hormone that binds to and activates the insulin receptor (InsR) and insulin-like growth factor one receptor (Igf1R) kinases to promote cell growth and proliferation in many cell types including cardiomyocytes (Bergman et al., 2013; Geng et al., 2017; Li et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: IGF2 promotes cell growth and proliferation in many cell types including cardiomyocytes.
source: IGF2 encodes a peptide hormone that binds to and activates the insulin receptor (InsR) and insulin-like growth factor one receptor (Igf1R) kinases to promote cell growth and proliferation in many cell types including cardiomyocytes (Bergman et al., 2013; Geng et al., 2017; Li et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The functional product of the H19 gene is a 2.3 kb long non-coding RNA.
source: In contrast, the functional product of the H19 gene is a 2.3 kb long non-coding RNA whose biochemical functions remain controversial (Brannan et al., 1990; Gabory et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The biochemical functions of H19 lncRNA remain controversial.
source: In contrast, the functional product of the H19 gene is a 2.3 kb long non-coding RNA whose biochemical functions remain controversial (Brannan et al., 1990; Gabory et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field supported by citations.

claim: H19 lncRNA acts as the precursor for microRNAs (Mir675-3p and Mir675-5p).
source: Reported roles for the H19 lncRNA include (1) acting as the precursor for microRNAs (Mir675-3p and Mir675-5p) (Cai and Cullen, 2007; Keniry et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a reported role supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: H19 lncRNA regulates the bioavailability of Mirlet7 (let-7) microRNAs.
source: (2) regulating the bioavailability of Mirlet7 (let-7) microRNAs (Gao et al., 2014; Geng et al., 2018; Kallen et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a reported role supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: H19 lncRNA interacts with p53 protein to reduce its function.
source: (3) interacting with p53 protein to reduce its function (Hadji et al., 2016; Park et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a reported role supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: H19 lncRNA regulates DNA methylation to thereby modulate gene expression.
source: (4) regulating DNA methylation to thereby modulate gene expression (Zhou et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a reported role supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In humans, disruption of the maternally inherited H19ICR results in biallelic IGF2 along with reduced H19 expression.
source: In humans, disruption of the maternally inherited H19ICR results in biallelic IGF2 along with reduced H19 expression and is associated with the developmental disorder, Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) (Jacob et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Disruption of the maternally inherited H19ICR is associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS).
source: In humans, disruption of the maternally inherited H19ICR results in biallelic IGF2 along with reduced H19 expression and is associated with the developmental disorder, Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) (Jacob et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: BWS is a fetal overgrowth disorder.
source: BWS is a fetal overgrowth disorder but the specific manifestations of overgrowth vary between patients.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about BWS.

claim: The specific manifestations of overgrowth in BWS vary between patients.
source: BWS is a fetal overgrowth disorder but the specific manifestations of overgrowth vary between patients.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about BWS.

claim: Cardiomegaly is a common newborn presentation in BWS but typically resolves without treatment.
source: Cardiomegaly is a common newborn presentation but typically resolves without treatment.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about BWS.

claim: Cardiomyopathies in BWS include ventricular dilation, valve/septal defects, fibrotic and rhabdomyoma tumors, and vascular abnormalities.
source: Cardiomyopathies are rarer and include ventricular dilation, valve/septal defects, fibrotic and rhabdomyoma tumors, and vascular abnormalities (Cohen, 2005; Descartes et al., 2008; Drut et al., 2006; Elliott et al., 1994; Greenwood et al., 1977; Knopp et al., 2015; Longardt et al., 2014; Ryan et al., 1989; Satgé et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: BWS incidence correlates with artificial reproductive technologies (ART).
source: BWS incidence correlates with artificial reproductive technologies (ART) (DeBaun et al., 2003; Gicquel et al., 2003; Halliday et al., 2004; Hattori et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2018; Maher et al., 2003; Mussa et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Among BWS patients, the frequency of heart defects is higher in those born via ART.
source: and among BWS patients, the frequency of heart defects is higher in those born via ART (Tenorio et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Deletion of the H19ICR on the maternal chromosome results in biallelic Igf2 and reduced levels of H19 in mice.
source: That is, deletion of the H19ICR on the maternal chromosome results in biallelic Igf2 and reduced levels of H19.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: The LOI mouse model displays cardiovascular defects seen in BWS patients.
source: In this study, we show that the LOI mouse model displays cardiovascular defects seen in BWS patients.
evidence: This is supported by echocardiography and histological data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: During fetal development, increased circulating IGF2 activates AKT/mTOR pathways in cardiomyocytes resulting in cellular hypertrophy and hyperplasia.
source: During fetal development, increased circulating IGF2 activates AKT/mTOR pathways in cardiomyocytes resulting in cellular hypertrophy and hyperplasia.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data showing increased phosphorylated AKT and S6K1, and by experiments with IGF2 peptide and pathway inhibitors.

claim: Neonatal hypertrophy in LOI mice is transient, non-pathologic, and unaffected by the presence or absence of a functional H19 gene.
source: This neonatal hypertrophy is transient, non-pathologic, and unaffected by the presence or absence of a functional H19 gene.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that LOI+H19 BAC mice still show neonatal hypertrophy, and that heart size normalizes by 2 months.

claim: Loss of H19 lncRNA results in cardiac fibrosis and hypertrophy and a progressive cardiac pathology in adult animals.
source: However, loss of H19 lncRNA results in cardiac fibrosis and hypertrophy and a progressive cardiac pathology in adult animals.
evidence: This is supported by data from H19ΔEx1/H19+ mice showing progressive cardiac pathologies.

claim: In both neonatal and adult hearts, H19 lncRNA expression is restricted to endothelial cells (ECs).
source: In both neonatal and adult hearts, H19 lncRNA expression is restricted to endothelial cells (ECs).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Loss of H19 results in high incidence of ECs that co-express endothelial and mesenchymal markers in vivo.
source: In vivo, loss of H19 results in high incidence of ECs that co-express endothelial and mesenchymal markers.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Primary cardiac endothelial cells can be driven toward a mesenchymal phenotype by manipulating H19 expression levels.
source: Similarly, primary cardiac endothelial cells can be driven toward a mesenchymal phenotype by manipulating H19 expression levels.
evidence: This is supported by transfection experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: H19 lncRNA acts by regulating Mirlet7 bioavailability.
source: Finally, we describe structure–function analyses in two novel mouse models (Figure 1B) and show that H19 lncRNA acts by regulating Mirlet7 bioavailability.
evidence: This is supported by data from H19ΔLet7 mice and RNA pull-down experiments.

claim: Hearts isolated from P1 LOI mice display cellular hyperplasia.
source: Hearts isolated from P1 LOI mice display cellular hyperplasia and cellular hypertrophy. Hyperplasia is indicated by increased staining for Ki-67 (a marker for cell proliferation) in tissue sections (Figure 2A,C) and by increased levels of Ki-67 and of cyclins E1 and D1 in protein extracts (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Ki-67 staining and immunoblot data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Hearts isolated from P1 LOI mice display cellular hypertrophy.
source: Hearts isolated from P1 LOI mice display cellular hyperplasia and cellular hypertrophy.
evidence: This is supported by measurements of cardiomyocyte surface areas shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Neonatal LOI hearts do not display increased fibrosis or expression of protein markers associated with heart disease.
source: Apart from their increased size, neonatal LOI hearts do not display any obvious pathologies. For example, we did not see increased fibrosis or expression of protein markers associated with heart disease.
evidence: This is based on histological and immunoblot analyses of neonatal hearts.

claim: By 2 months of age, LOI mice cannot be distinguished from wild-type by cardiomegaly as measured by heart weight/tibia length ratios.
source: Furthermore, by 2 months of age, we were unable to distinguish LOI mice by cardiomegaly as measured by heart weight/tibia length ratios: WT = 6.7 ± 0.3 mg/mm (N = 8), LOI = 6.8 ± 0.3 mg/mm (N = 13), p=0.79 (Student's t-test).
evidence: This is supported by direct measurements of heart weight/tibia length ratios.

claim: By 6 months, LOI mice displayed cardiac hypertrophy as measured by a 28% increase in heart weight/tibia length ratios.
source: By 6 months, LOI mice displayed cardiac hypertrophy as measured by a 28% increase in heart weight/tibia length ratios (wild type = 10.0 ± 1.7 mg/mm, N = 8; LOI = 12.8 ± 0.2 mg/mm, N = 10; p=0.005).
evidence: This is supported by direct measurements of heart weight/tibia length ratios.

claim: Transverse sections from 6-month-old LOI mice revealed increased fiber diameter.
source: Transverse sections revealed increased fiber diameter in LOI hearts (wild type = 10.2 ± 0.7 μm; LOI = 14.4 ± 0.8 μm; p=0.007) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by histological measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LOI mice show increased levels of ANP, Myh7, cleaved Caspase-3, cleaved Caspase-7, and cleaved PARP proteins by 1 year of age.
source: The hypertrophy in LOI mice might be considered pathologic based on increased levels of ANP, Myh7, cleaved Caspase-3, cleaved Caspase-7, and cleaved PARP proteins as well as decreased levels of Serca2 protein in all LOI mice by 1 year of age (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Mitra et al., 2013; van Empel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LOI mice show decreased levels of Serca2 protein by 1 year of age.
source: The hypertrophy in LOI mice might be considered pathologic based on increased levels of ANP, Myh7, cleaved Caspase-3, cleaved Caspase-7, and cleaved PARP proteins as well as decreased levels of Serca2 protein in all LOI mice by 1 year of age (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Mitra et al., 2013; van Empel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both interstitial and perivascular fibrosis are prominent in LOI animals by 6 months of age.
source: Finally, both interstitial and perivascular fibrosis are prominent in LOI animals by 6 months of age (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Masson's trichrome staining shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Left ventricles from 13-month-old LOI mice are dilated as measured by increased LV volumes at both systole and diastole.
source: Left ventricles (LV) from LOI mice are dilated (as measured by increased LV volumes at both systole and diastole), mildly hypertrophic (as measured by increased wall thickness, LVAW diastole and LVPW diastole), and show diminished function (as measured by reduced ejection fractions, % EF).
evidence: This is supported by echocardiography data shown in Table 1.

claim: Left ventricles from 13-month-old LOI mice are mildly hypertrophic as measured by increased wall thickness.
source: Left ventricles (LV) from LOI mice are dilated (as measured by increased LV volumes at both systole and diastole), mildly hypertrophic (as measured by increased wall thickness, LVAW diastole and LVPW diastole), and show diminished function (as measured by reduced ejection fractions, % EF).
evidence: This is supported by echocardiography data shown in Table 1.

claim: Left ventricles from 13-month-old LOI mice show diminished function as measured by reduced ejection fractions.
source: Left ventricles (LV) from LOI mice are dilated (as measured by increased LV volumes at both systole and diastole), mildly hypertrophic (as measured by increased wall thickness, LVAW diastole and LVPW diastole), and show diminished function (as measured by reduced ejection fractions, % EF).
evidence: This is supported by echocardiography data shown in Table 1.

claim: LOI mice showed large increases in velocity and turbulence of blood flow from the LV outflow tract.
source: LOI mice showed large increases in velocity and turbulence of blood flow from the LV outflow tract.
evidence: This is supported by echocardiography data shown in Table 1.

claim: Major vessel lumen diameters were >30% larger in LOI mice.
source: Finally, major vessel lumen diameters (measured at the aortic arch and the first brachial arch) were >30% larger in LOI mice.
evidence: This is supported by echocardiography data shown in Table 1.

claim: Neonatal hypertrophy and hyperplasia occurs in both male and female LOI pups.
source: However, neonatal hypertrophy and hyperplasia occurs in both male and female pups.
evidence: This is based on observations of neonatal phenotypes in both sexes.

claim: Adult LOI females consistently showed relatively weak cardiac phenotypes with non-significant p-values.
source: Note that results shown in Figure 3 and in Table 1 describe comparisons of age-matched male mice. Adult LOI females consistently showed relatively weak phenotypes and p-values were not significant (data now shown).
evidence: This is based on echocardiography analyses of female mice.

claim: An H19 BAC transgene that restores normal H19 expression does not prevent neonatal cardiomegaly in LOI mice.
source: First, we rescued H19 expression in an LOI background by introducing a 140 kb H19 Bacterial Artificial Chromosome (H19 BAC) (Kaffer et al., 2001; Kaffer et al., 2000; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) but still saw cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and hyperplasia in neonates (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by histological and immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: Loss of H19 in a background where Igf2 remains monoallelic does not result in neonatal cardiomyocyte hypertrophy or hyperplasia.
source: Second, we tested the effect of removing H19 in a background where Igf2 remains monoallelic by comparing H19ΔEx1/H19+ (Figure 1B) with wild-type littermates. (Reduced expression of H19 lncRNA in H19ΔEx1/H19+ is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.) Loss of H19 lncRNA does not result in neonatal cardiomyocyte hypertrophy or hyperplasia (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Neonatal hypertrophy in LOI mice is dependent only upon biallelic (2× dosage) Igf2 transcription.
source: Altogether, we conclude that loss of H19 lncRNA does not contribute to neonatal hypergrowth. Rather, this neonatal hypertrophy is dependent only upon biallelic (2× dosage) Igf2 transcription.
evidence: This conclusion is based on genetic experiments comparing different mouse models.

claim: Hearts from LOI neonates show increased levels of phosphorylated AKT and of phosphorylated S6K1.
source: Consistent with a critical role for AKT/mTOR signaling in LOI-dependent neonatal hypertrophy, hearts from LOI neonates show increased levels of phosphorylated AKT and of phosphorylated S6K1, a downstream marker for mTORC1 activity (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The LOI cellular hypertrophy and pAKT hyperactivation phenotypes can be phenocopied by treatment of wild-type primary cardiomyocytes with IGF2 peptide.
source: Moreover, the LOI cellular hypertrophy and pAKT hyperactivation phenotypes can be phenocopied by treatment of wild-type primary cardiomyocytes with IGF2 peptide.
evidence: This is supported by experiments shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: IGF2 action on cardiomyocytes is blocked by BMS-754807, a specific inhibitor of the receptor kinase.
source: However, IGF2 action is blocked by BMS-754807, a specific inhibitor of the receptor kinase, or by treatment with rapamycin, an mTOR signaling pathway inhibitor (Figure 2G and H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experiments shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: IGF2 action on cardiomyocytes is blocked by rapamycin, an mTOR signaling pathway inhibitor.
source: However, IGF2 action is blocked by BMS-754807, a specific inhibitor of the receptor kinase, or by treatment with rapamycin, an mTOR signaling pathway inhibitor (Figure 2G and H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experiments shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: Expression of Igf2 is low in the heart relative to other tissues, especially liver and skeletal muscle.
source: In fact, expression of Igf2 is low in the heart relative to other tissues, especially liver and skeletal muscle (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), which are believed to be the major source of circulating IGF2 peptide.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Liver and skeletal muscle are believed to be the major source of circulating IGF2 peptide.
source: In fact, expression of Igf2 is low in the heart relative to other tissues, especially liver and skeletal muscle (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), which are believed to be the major source of circulating IGF2 peptide.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cardiomyocyte-specific ICR deletion does not cause hypertrophy in neonatal mice.
source: Cardiomyocyte-specific ICR deletion does not cause hypertrophy. Rather, H19ICRFlox/H19+ Myh6 Cre mice were indistinguishable from their wild-type littermates (Figure 2E,F,I,J; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data from cardiomyocyte-specific deletion experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The effects of LOI on neonatal cardiomyocytes are cell non-autonomous.
source: Note that our data demonstrate that the effects of LOI on neonatal cardiomyocytes are cell non-autonomous but do not rule out a cell autonomous role in other cell types, including cardiac endothelium.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cardiomyocyte-specific deletion experiments.

claim: The H19 BAC transgene successfully prevents adult cardiac pathologies in LOI mice.
source: While the H19 BAC transgene does not prevent neonatal cardiomegaly, it does successfully prevent adult pathologies. That is, hearts from 6 month LOI mice carrying the H19 transgene are not enlarged as determined by heart weight/tibia length ratios (LOI = 12.9 ± 0.6 mg/mm, N = 3; LOI+ H19 BAC transgene = 11.5 ± 0.7, N = 3; p<0.05), are not fibrotic (Figure 4A,B), and do not express cardiomyopathy markers (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by measurements and histological data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Loss of H19 is necessary to induce LOI cardiomyopathies.
source: Thus, loss of H19 is necessary to induce LOI cardiomyopathies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the H19 BAC rescue experiments.

claim: 6-month-old H19ΔEx1/H19+ mice display LOI cardiac pathologies including hypertrophy, fibrosis, and expression of disease markers.
source: Yet, 6-month-old H19ΔEx1/H19+ mice display LOI cardiac pathologies including hypertrophy (Figure 4D), fibrosis (Figure 4E,F), and expression of disease markers (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by histological and immunoblot data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Neonatal cardiomegaly is not a risk factor for adult pathologies in LOI mice.
source: Thus, neonatal cardiomegaly is not a risk factor for adult pathologies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that LOI+H19 BAC mice show neonatal hypertrophy but not adult pathologies, while H19ΔEx1/H19+ mice show adult pathologies without neonatal hypertrophy.

claim: In fetal and neonatal hearts, H19 is expressed in all endothelial cells including microvasculature.
source: In fetal and neonatal hearts H19 is expressed in all endothelial cells including microvasculature.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In adult hearts, H19 expression is patchy and patterns vary between mice but are always restricted to endocardium and endothelial cells lining major coronary vessels.
source: In adults, H19 expression is patchy and patterns vary between mice but are always restricted to endocardium and endothelial cells lining major coronary vessels (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In coronary vessels, H19 RNA expression exclusively overlapped with endothelial specific marker von-Willebrand's factor.
source: For example, in coronary vessels, H19 RNA expression exclusively overlapped with endothelial specific marker von-Willebrand's factor (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by combined in situ and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RNA sequencing identified 228 differentially expressed genes in H19-deficient endothelial cells with adjusted p-values of <0.1.
source: RNA sequencing identified 228 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with adjusted p-values of <0.1, including 111 upregulated and 117 downregulated transcripts (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: GO analysis of differentially expressed genes in H19-deficient endothelial cells gives evidence for a change in cellular identity.
source: GO analysis for biological, cellular, and molecular pathways gives evidence for a change in cellular identity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Enriched biological pathways in H19-deficient endothelial cells included positive regulation of mesenchymal cell proliferation, positive regulation of endothelial cell migration, and cell adhesion.
source: Specifically, enriched biological pathways included positive regulation of mesenchymal cell proliferation, positive regulation of endothelial cell migration, and cell adhesion (n = 36, p-adj = 0.003).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Cellular pathways in H19-deficient endothelial cells showed enrichment for genes coding for extracellular matrix.
source: Cellular pathways showed enrichment for genes coding for extracellular matrix (n = 42, p-adj = 1.83E-10).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Enriched molecular function categories in H19-deficient endothelial cells include extracellular matrix binding and TGFβ binding.
source: Enriched molecular function categories include extracellular matrix binding and TGFβ binding (n = 7, p-adj = 0.0001; n = 5, p-adj = 0.1), as well as other pathways that are especially active during endothelial to mesenchymal transition (EndMT).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: 63 differentially expressed genes in H19-deficient endothelial cells were implicated in EndMT as either players in driving the transition or as markers.
source: EndMT is not an identifiable GO term, however, we conducted a PubMed search of the 188 DEGs described in the PubMed literature database and noted that 63 DEGs were implicated in EndMT as either players in driving the transition or as markers.
evidence: This is based on a literature search of differentially expressed genes.

claim: H19 expression reduces expression of a mesenchymal cell marker (SM22α) in primary endothelial cells.
source: H19 expression reduces expression of a mesenchymal cell marker (SM22α) and of genes encoding transcription factors critical for EndMT (Snail and Slug) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by transfection experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: H19 expression reduces expression of genes encoding transcription factors critical for EndMT (Snail and Slug) in primary endothelial cells.
source: H19 expression reduces expression of a mesenchymal cell marker (SM22α) and of genes encoding transcription factors critical for EndMT (Snail and Slug) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by transfection experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: EndMT is an essential part of the normal development of many tissues/organs including heart.
source: EndMT is an essential part of the normal development of many tissues/organs including heart.
evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: EndMT is critical in cardiac valve development.
source: For example, EndMT is critical in cardiac valve development (Kisanuki et al., 2001; Markwald et al., 1977).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EndMT contributes to cardiac diseases including cardiac fibrosis, valve calcification, and endocardial elastofibrosis.
source: Studies also report that EndMT contributes to cardiac diseases including cardiac fibrosis, valve calcification, and endocardial elastofibrosis (Evrard et al., 2016; Goumans et al., 2008; Piera-Velazquez et al., 2011; Zeisberg et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: H19 lncRNA is known to physically bind Mirlet7g (let-7g) and Mirlet7i (let-7i) in exon one and Mirlet7e (let-7e) in exon four in mice.
source: H19 lncRNA is known to physically bind Mirlet7g (let-7g) and Mirlet7i (let-7i) in exon one and Mirlet7e (let-7e) in exon four in mice (Kallen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mirlet7 miRNAs play a role in cardiovascular diseases including cardiac hypertrophy, cardiac fibrosis, dilated cardiomyopathy, and myocardial infarction.
source: Mirlet7 miRNAs are known to play a role in cardiovascular diseases including cardiac hypertrophy, cardiac fibrosis, dilated cardiomyopathy, and myocardial infarction (Bao et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mice carrying the H19ΔLet7 mutation express H19 at wild-type levels.
source: Mice carrying this mutation (H19ΔLet7/ H19ΔLet7) express H19 at wild-type levels (Figure 6B), which shows that the deletions do not disrupt lncRNA expression or stability.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: H19 and Mirlet7 RNAs physically associate in cells.
source: These experiments provided direct biochemical evidence that H19 and Mirlet7 RNAs do physically associate and also that these interactions are lost in our H19Δlet7 deletion model (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA pull-down experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: H19 and Mirlet7 RNA interactions are lost in the H19Δlet7 deletion model.
source: These experiments provided direct biochemical evidence that H19 and Mirlet7 RNAs do physically associate and also that these interactions are lost in our H19Δlet7 deletion model (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA pull-down experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: One year old H19ΔLet7/H19ΔLet7 mice displayed cardiomegaly as measured by a 32% increase in heart weight/tibia length ratios.
source: One year old H19ΔLet7/H19ΔLet7 mice displayed cardiomegaly as measured by a 32% increase in heart weight/tibia length ratios (wild type = 7.5 ± 1.7 mg/mm, N = 4; H19ΔLet7/H19+ = 9.9 ± 2.2 mg/mm, N = 5; p=0.007).
evidence: This is supported by direct measurements of heart weight/tibia length ratios.

claim: The cardiac hypertrophy in H19ΔLet7/H19ΔLet7 mice was accompanied by increased interstitial and perivascular fibrosis.
source: The cardiac hypertrophy in H19ΔLet7/H19ΔLet7 mice was accompanied by increased interstitial and perivascular fibrosis (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: H19ΔLet7/H19ΔLet7 mice show increased levels of cardiomyopathy markers.
source: The pathologic nature of the observed cardiac myopathies in these mutant mice was confirmed by the increased levels of cardiomyopathy markers (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: More than 50% of BWS cases are associated with epigenetic lesions that disrupt expression of CDKN1C.
source: More than 50% of BWS cases are associated with epigenetic lesions that disrupt expression of CDKN1C, an imprinted gene closely linked to IGF2/H19 but under control of its own ICR (IC2).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about BWS molecular etiology.

claim: About 5% of BWS cases are associated with disrupted imprinting at the IGF2/H19 locus.
source: About 5% of BWS cases are associated with disrupted imprinting at the IGF2/H19 locus.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about BWS molecular etiology.

claim: About 20% of BWS cases are associated with paternal uniparental disomy of the entire region.
source: About 20% of cases are associated with paternal uniparental disomy of the entire region (potentially affecting both CDKN1C and IGF2/H19) (IC1 and IC2), and another 20% of cases are of unknown origin.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about BWS molecular etiology.

claim: Recent studies suggest a 6- to 10-fold increased risk for BWS specifically because of the increased chance that IGF2/H19 imprinting is disrupted in ART.
source: However, more recent studies have examined the effect of ART on epigenetic changes (Odom and Segars, 2010) and suggest a 6- to 10-fold increased risk for BWS specifically because of the increased chance that IGF2/H19 imprinting is disrupted (Hattori et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2018; Mussa et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: In the mouse LOI model, disease phenotypes are not restricted to fetal and neonatal stages.
source: Thus, in the mouse LOI model, disease phenotypes are not restricted to fetal and neonatal stages.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation of progressive adult phenotypes in LOI mice.

claim: H19 RNA levels play a role in modulating EC fate decisions, so that cells lacking H19 are modestly but measurably more likely to switch toward a transitional state.
source: Rather, our data indicate that H19 RNA levels play a role in modulating the fate decision, so that cells lacking H19 are modestly but measurably more likely to switch toward a transitional state where both EC and mesenchymal markers are expressed.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the EndMT frequency data.

claim: The observed 50% reduction in expression of TGFβ receptors might be a key phenotype in H19-deficient ECs.
source: It is interesting to note one commonality of key pathways disrupted by loss of H19 lncRNA is that they share regulation by TGFβ signaling, suggesting that the observed 50 % reduction in expression of TGFβ receptors might be a key phenotype in H19-deficient ECs (Goumans et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculation based on pathway analysis and supported by a citation.

claim: In vitro studies of H19 in cancer cells find EMT is induced by increasing H19 RNA.
source: However, in contrast to our findings that activation of mesenchymal expression is associated with loss of H19, these in vitro analyses find EMT is induced by increasing H19 RNA.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature findings.

claim: In neonatal ECs, H19 lncRNA represents about 1% of all polyadenylated RNA.
source: H19 can be a very abundant transcript. In neonatal ECs, H19 lncRNA represents about 1% of all polyadenylated RNA.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data from isolated endothelial cells.

claim: H19ΔEx1/H19+ mice have 100× reduced levels of lncRNA but almost normal levels of Mir675-3p and -5p.
source: Here we show that H19ΔEx1/H19+ have 100× reduced levels of lncRNA but almost normal levels of Mir675-3p and -5 p and still show cardiac pathology.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The fibrosis phenotype in H19ΔLet7 mice is more intense relative to that seen in an H19 null.
source: We find the fibrosis phenotype in H19ΔLet7 mice to be especially interesting. We speculate that intensity relative to that seen in an H19 null is most consistent with the idea that H19 lncRNA has multiple roles in the cell and by disrupting only one role we have altered some balance, so that the animal is worse off than having no H19 at all.
evidence: This is based on comparison of fibrosis severity between different mutant models.

claim: Multiple studies of Mirlet7 function in hearts indicate that Mirlet7 functions as an anti-fibrotic factor.
source: The strong phenotype in H19ΔLet7 mice is consistent with several previous studies that emphasize the importance of H19 lncRNA interactions with Mirlet7 miRNAs but it is also paradoxical in that multiple studies of Mirlet7 function in hearts indicate that Mirlet7 functions as an anti-fibrotic factor. That is, reduced Mirlet7 is a risk factor for fibrosis and fibrosis induces Mirlet7, presumably as a corrective measure (Bao et al., 2013; Elliot et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: H19 and Igf2 are generally thought of as fetal genes since their expression is so strongly repressed after birth.
source: H19 and Igf2 are generally thought of as fetal genes since their expression is so strongly repressed after birth.
evidence: This is established knowledge about H19 and Igf2 expression patterns.

claim: Even after 100-fold developmentally regulated decrease, H19 remains one of the top 100 genes in terms of RNA levels.
source: However, as already mentioned, at peak expression, H19 levels are extraordinarily high. Thus, even after 100-fold developmentally regulated decrease, H19 remains one of the top 100 genes in terms of RNA levels.
evidence: This is based on RNA expression data from the manuscript.
